reviewer: Claude agent review (Opus), not a human historian
text: 2026-10-23: the book was rewritten to the storytelling template (README §6) and approved on an independent review against facts.json (36 facts), research/mysuru-verified.md, Hayavadana Rao vol. I on archive.org, the published story and review, and all thirteen pictures. Four named people and four years in the prose, NFC, no em dashes, the turning point at scene 10, every scene ending on a question, and alt texts true to the frames.

Seven blockers were found and fixed: the 'kingdom of one fort' wording, fixed in the last review, had come back and is gone again; scene 6 now tells the Maratha commanders' capture, killing, mutilation and heads plainly; scene 10 follows the Kannada works' fight at the walls before terms (HR pp. 306–307) instead of an invented order not to strike first; an undisclosed claim about officers in the hill forts was cut; scene 2's sixteen days no longer contradict themselves; Doddaiya's later appointment as Dalavai is disclosed; his upbringing in Mysore and his father as the king's elder brother are now sourced to HR pp. 212, 253 and 269 (f-birth and research §2a updated).

Newcomer test (README §7): (1) yes, a first-time reader can say who Chikkadevaraja was, what he wanted (one state between great powers) and why it matters; (2) yes, the torch-oxen night, the dying minister's choice and the fight before Bengaluru carry the suspense, and the cost (the taxes, the Nanjangud night, the murdered friend) is told before the turn.

2026-10-12: approved on a third read of story.json (introduction, twelve scenes with titles, alt texts, paragraphs, facts and dramatised lists, summary, ನಿಮಗೆ ಗೊತ್ತೇ?, visitToday, provenance, disclosure, content note), facts.json and the collections.json 'mysuru' entry. The first pass returned seventeen text blockers; the second pass returned one fact blocker and one image blocker; all are fixed.

First-pass blockers, fixed: (1) the introduction said today's historians reject the Nanjangud story; it, the summary and the content note now say Wilks believed it, Hayavadana Rao rejected it, and historians have no consensus. (2) scene-01 weighed the evidence in the prose ('ಕಥೆ ಹಾಗೆ. ಖಚಿತವಾದದ್ದು ಇಷ್ಟು'); now an in-story line. (3) scene-02 compared the palace annals with the stones; now the court poets' Yadu descent (Govinda Vaidya 1648). (4) scene-03 credited the troop figures to Chokkanatha's poets; now camp rumour, with Mallikarjuna's Sriranga-Mahatmya (1678) in the dramatised list instead of Tirumalarya. (5) an undisclosed 'not even a month' timing at Madhuvana; cut. (6) scene-05 called the king a Vishnu devotee in 1677, against scene-09's 1686 profession; and a Vardhamana chaityalaya with no source; both cut. (7) Shahaji's jagirs (Bengaluru, Hoskote, Doddaballapur, Sira) taken by Shivaji, found only in the unverified notes and at odds with Ekoji selling Bengaluru in 1687; cut. (8) 'ಅವರು ನಂಬಿದ್ದು ತಪ್ಪು' and a claim that the 1686 plate carries the title Apratima-Vira; cut, and the title now credited to the Apratima-Vira-Charitam and the 1722 Srirangapatna inscription. (9) scene-06 cited the plate in the prose; the Ramayana comparison is now told at court; the date dispute now says Wilks 1697 only. (10) scene-07 claimed the Jesuit letter said 'only' fire and sword; rewritten; Wilks's twenty taxes and the Annals' nineteen separated; unsourced Hayavadana Rao claims ('revival', 'exaggerated') cut. (11) an invented suspicion on the palegars cut; the 1693 namam order corrected to courtiers who were 'desired' to wear it (HR p. 359). (12) scene-11 put the first council at Hangala; now the coronation-day council. (13) the Binnapam and Gita-Gopalam were both called prose; now 'petitions in Kannada'; 'thirty-one years ago an island' now 'one of several kingdoms on the Kaveri'. (14) a dead Commons link for Melkote replaced. (15) unsourced details cut: Doddaiya as nephew, 1680 and March–May 1682, Sambhaji at Trichy, Devaraja 'without issue', 'only son', two titles, Tumkur and Hoskote, the ephemeris, the ivory throne in 1799, the canal date. (16) f-accession cited the death-date reference; now HR p. 272 fn 12. (17) the dynasty entry called the 1659–1673 king ದೊಡ್ಡದೇವರಾಜ, the name the story gives his brother, Chikkadevaraja's father; now ದೇವರಾಜ ಒಡೆಯರ್ with a note, and unsourced Bednur, inn, 'first mint', noon and morning details gone.

Second-pass blocker, fixed: f-conquests had lost its Rice citation while keeping Rice's sentence as its quote; the source is again Rice, Mysore Gazetteer I (1897) p. 368 with Wilks I pp. 93–94, the sentence is now transcribed in research/mysuru-verified.md §7, and scene-10's dramatised list credits Rice and Wilks.

The storytelling rule checked: scene prose has no 'historians think', 'the plate says', 'disputed' or scholar name. The ಐತಿಹ್ಯ framing of the astrology tale in scene-01 is the README's legend label and reads in-world; the last sentence of scene-08 ('ಕೇಳಿದವನು ಅದನ್ನು ನಂಬಿ ಬರೆದಿಟ್ಟ') alludes to Wilks without naming him and reads as story. Every choice is disclosed in its scene: Hangala c. 1668 (HR) against confinement in the previous reign (Wilks, Rice); Visalaksha met at Hangala; the sixteen days and the same-day council; Madhuvana's undated battle and the poets' figures; Shivaji's horse rather than Shivaji, the Kannada works' repulse chosen over the Bombay rumour; 1682 over Wilks's 1697; one torch per ox in prose, two in the picture; the Nanjangud night as Wilks's tradition with Rice, Hayavadana Rao, Devachandra and the Jesuit letter on the evidence page; the night, palanquin and unnamed assassin; the face-off and terms at Bengaluru between Wilks's purchase and the Kannada works' fight, without saying who got the money; the Mughal honours as Mysore's record with Hayavadana Rao's 'no independent evidence' and the 200-rupee footnote; Wilks's Ahmednagar not named in the prose; the Melkote steps and the eclipse's dimness as invention.

Checked against research/mysuru-verified.md: birth 22 Sep 1645; marriages Feb 1662; Hangala c. 1668–1673; accession 28 Feb 1673, sixteen days after Devaraja's death, in his 28th year, with the variants 5 Mar, 1672 and 16 Oct; the five-man council; 5 Mar 1673, Dhuligote to Salem, Madhuvana, the Sendamangalam forest; the post and spies (Wilks p. 89, HR p. 337) and Hyder; the palegars brought to the capital (Wilks p. 205); 5 Mar 1677 at Shravanabelagola; Shivaji in August 1677 and the Bombay letter of 24 Aug; Trichy 1682, 'horrible butchery', Kumaraiya taken, 26 May 1682; Kottatti and Honnalagere, Dadaji, Jaitaji, Nimbaji, two to three thousand transport oxen, the heads on the Mysore Gate, the Panchavati verse of EC III Sr 14; Wilks's twenty taxes, the Annals' nineteen, soldiers' lands exempt, the inverted plough; the 1686 Jesuit letter; Nanjangud: about four hundred, tent-walled squares, the pit, more than seven hundred maths, orange robes, Wilks's 'entire belief', Rice's acceptance, Hayavadana Rao's rejection and his partiality, Devachandra's Tayur story; Visalaksha's murder in 1686, not earlier than July, Naganna, Yechiganahalli as rakta-kodige, Tirumalaiyangar named; Bengaluru 1687: Ekoji, three lakhs, Qasim Khan's forced marches, 10 and 14 July, Wilks's four days, Orme's August, Pootia's 29 July, Sira, Db 31 of 1691, 'friend and protector', d. 1698; Bn 118 of 1705; the embassy 1699–1700 under Lingannaiya, the procession, Ranganatha's feet, Jug Deo Raj / Raja-Jagadev, 'no independent evidence', two hundred rupees and 'Zemindar'; eighteen departments c. 1700 (HR pp. 355–358) with Devachandra's 1686; two thousand pagodas after the bath and namam, Navakoti Narayana; Chikkadevaraja-sagara, Deva-nala and the 1701 Jesuit mole; the writings and their dates; HR pp. 392 and 501 on dress and looks; titles; death 16 Nov 1704 with the eclipse (Tarana Karttika ba. 30), 60th year, 32nd of the reign, no sati, Wilks's 12 Dec, Rice's 76; the Muka Arasu and Tirumalaiyangar's year and a half; Palni and Anemale to Midagesi, Baramahal to Coorg and Balam, 1,323,571 Kanthirai pagodas.

Kannada: adult told-story register; no em dash; NFC in story.json, facts.json and collections.json; Kannada digits in prose; ತಿರುಮಲಾರ್ಯ joined to ತಿರುಮಲೈಯಂಗಾರ್ at first use in scene-02 ('ಆಸ್ಥಾನದಲ್ಲಿ ತಿರುಮಲೈಯಂಗಾರ್') and used consistently after; ವರಹ for pagoda. story.facts is identical to facts.json (36 facts); every scene facts[] id and didYouKnow id resolves and every fact is used. The content note (war, the mention of mutilated commanders, a minister's murder, the crushing of a tax rising, the Nanjangud tradition) is truthful; the mutilation is not narrated in any scene and is a single word (ಅಂಗಚ್ಛೇದ / mutilated) in f-sr14-plate; the Jangamas appear as the farmers' teachers and as victims, never as villains, and the content note says nothing is said against any community.

Mysuru dynasty entry checked against research/mysuru.md §1 and mysuru-verified.md §1: Yaduraya 1399 as tradition and first records c. 1550; capital Mysore, Srirangapatna 1610–1799, Mysore again; Raja Wodeyar 1578–1617 and 8 Feb 1610; Kanthirava Narasaraja 1638–1659, the 1639 siege and coins in his own name; Devaraja Wodeyar 1659–1673 as Chikkadevaraja's uncle ('Dodda Deva-Raja' in the palace list); Chikkadevaraja 1673–1704; the Muka Arasu 1704–1714 (1713 in Rice's list, noted); Krishnaraja II 1734–1766 and Hyder c. 1761; Krishnaraja III from 30 June 1799; the commissioners 1831–1881 and the Rendition of 25 March 1881; Krishnaraja IV 1895–1940; 1947. The dating note now says only the main rulers are listed.
illustrations: All thirteen WebPs (cover, scene-01 to scene-12, 1600x900, each under 200 KB) were opened and compared with their scene paragraphs, alt texts and bible/style.md, with enlarged crops of the faces, flags, the seal, the plough and the postmaster. scene-02 and scene-07 were re-encoded under the size budget after the first pass, and scene-10 was regenerated after the second; this approval hashes the current files.

Image blocker on the second pass, fixed: scene-10's Mughal standard was a green field with a white crescent on a crescent finial, which read as the modern Pakistan flag and as an anachronistic emblem; it is now a plain dark-green banner with a gold border on a spearhead finial, with no crescent or star anywhere in the picture.

Lead consistency: the same man in every picture that shows him, a long handsome face, a prominent straight nose, a thin curled moustache and a small pointed chin-beard, a white turban with a gold band and an emerald aigrette, a white gold-bordered angarkha and pearls: mounted before the island fort on the cover; on the elephant crossing the Kaveri (scene-02); leading the charge (scene-03); sallying on a grey horse (scene-05); at the Bengaluru gate (scene-10); on the temple steps (scene-11). Scene-01 shows him at 23 with hair in a knot and a moustache only; scene-12 shows him old with a white moustache and chin-beard and the Sri-Vaishnava mark. He is handsome, upright and dignified throughout.

cover: the king on a grey horse at sunset with a raised sword, red-turbaned riders and a Garuda banner, the island fort, the Ranganatha tower and the river. Nits: the sword is a curved talwar where the bible asks for a straight one; the banner Garuda is a spread heraldic bird.

scene-01: the young prince drawing a bow in a red-earth village yard at dawn, the young Brahmin with shaved forelock and palm leaves, the older Jain scholar in white, a stone well, tiled houses, blue hills. Nit: the straw target with painted rings looks modern.

scene-02: the king under an umbrella on a caparisoned elephant crossing the Kaveri at evening, old Kumaraiya in a red turban on horseback, drummers, the fort with cannon on its bastions and the temple tower. Nits: a Vaishnava mark painted on the elephant's forehead; the tower is taller than the 1670s one probably was.

scene-03: the king with a straight sword leading horsemen and matchlock men through a Madurai camp at dusk, an elephant with howdah, tents and fallen banners, boulder hills. Nit: the king wears a white-and-red upright mark in 1673 where the bible asks for a plain sandal mark before 1686.

scene-04: a post runner with a bell-staff and a torch-bearer running out of a village gate at night; inside, the postmaster writing by a lamp. Nit: he writes with a pen on flat sheets at a table rather than on a palm leaf as the alt says (paper is plausible for the period).

scene-05: the king sallying on a grey horse from the fort gate against Maratha light horse with saffron pennants and round shields, river and tower behind. Nits: a curved sword; the heraldic-bird Garuda banner.

scene-06: a long river of torch-horned oxen moving through the night fields, the Maratha tents turning toward it, Doddaiya's dark horsemen coming from behind. Two torches per ox, disclosed in the dramatised list.

scene-07: a wooden plough hung from a banyan at the village gate, red fields, farmers gathered round three saffron-robed teachers with rudraksha, shown with dignity. Nit: the plough reads only loosely as inverted.

scene-08: dusk outside a walled temple with a modest tower: a long dignified line of saffron-robed priests of all ages waiting at a cloth tent-wall enclosure, torches, guards, one priest being received. No violence, no pit, no blood.
scene-09: a narrow lamplit street at night, the palanquin set down and tilted, bearers fleeing, only the minister's arm visible inside, a single dark figure far down the street. No blood, no wound.

scene-10 (regenerated): the Bengaluru fort gate, a plain green Mughal banner and the Mysore Garuda flag on the gatehouse, bearded Qasim Khan in a flat Mughal turban and jama at left, the king with the namam at right, Mughal troops and red-turbaned Mysore troops at ease between them. Nit: the heraldic-bird Garuda.

scene-11: the procession at the Ranganatha temple: drums, the red ensign, gold trays carrying a round dark seal with illegible script and a silk robe, the bearer with horizontal ash lines, women in saris; the king on the steps. Nits: little grey at about 55; a tall tower.
scene-12: the old king writing with a stylus on a tied palm-leaf book on the steps of the Melkote hill temple at dawn, a brass lamp, the misty plain below. Clean.

No picture shows rockets, flintlocks with bayonets, uniforms, the present Mysore Palace, Tipu-era buildings, the present Nanjangud gopura, a tall kirita on the king, a crescent or star flag, modern letters, gore, a killing or a wound; no extra hands or fingers were found.
limitations: This is an AI review by a Claude agent; no human historian or epigraphist has read the text or checked the images.

Fact checking was limited to research/mysuru-verified.md and research/mysuru.md and did not re-fetch the primary editions. Several items rest only on Hayavadana Rao's paraphrase of Kannada works that no one on this project has read at first hand (Tirumalarya's Vamsavali, Vijayam and Apratima-Vira-Charitam, the Mysuru Dhoregala Purvabhyudaya, Devachandra's Rajavali-Kathe), and the Jesuit letters are known only as Hayavadana Rao quotes them.

The Nanjangud massacre is an oral tradition gathered by Wilks about 120 years later and is disputed; no contemporary record names Nanjangud. Hayavadana Rao's rejection comes from a palace-sponsored history openly partial to the king.

The Mughal honours of 1700 (the letter, the insignia, the Jagadeva Raja seal) rest on Mysore's own records and Wilks; no Mughal-side record or farman was found. The 200-rupee footnote is secondhand (Kirkpatrick's notes on the Asaf Jahi records). Wilks's Ahmednagar for the imperial camp in 1699 is doubtful and is not used in the prose.
Whether the solar eclipse of 16 November 1704 was visible at Srirangapatna was not checked; the dimming of the sky is the storyteller's.

No contemporary portrait of Chikkadevaraja is known; the palace miniature is probably a later copy and the Gundlupet relief has no published photograph. His face, every other face, the camps, the fort, the Nanjangud enclosure and the Bengaluru gate are invented, as the disclosure says.

Remaining small image nits were recorded and not regenerated: curved swords on the cover and in scene-05; heraldic-bird Garudas on the banners; the namam on the king in scene-03 and on the elephant in scene-02; the postmaster's paper in scene-04; little grey in scene-11; tall gopuras; the loosely inverted plough in scene-07; a modern-looking target in scene-01.
